prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) thoroughly. Let me start by fetching the official page and running several targeted searches.I have solid foundational information. Let me dig deeper into a few areas: the 2015 redesign, the COVID-19 supplements, typical users and research applications, and data archiving/preservation details.# Research Report: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)

**Verification of your provided information:** Your description is accurate. The title, URL, and description match the official CMS page nearly verbatim. A few factual refinements and a great deal of additional context follow below.

---

## 1. At a Glance

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Official title** | Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) |
| **Publisher / sponsor** | Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics (OEDA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) |
| **Data collection contractor** | NORC at the University of Chicago (current); Westat was the original field contractor |
| **Legal authority** | Section 1875 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. §1395ll) |
| **OMB clearance** | OMB No. 0938-0568 (Paperwork Reduction Act) |
| **In field since** | Fall 1991 (Round 1: September–December 1991); continuously in the field since then |
| **Scale** | 1.2+ million interviews completed; roughly 12,000–16,000 respondents annually; three interview rounds per year |
| **Primary URL** | https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey |
| **Free data portal** | data.cms.gov (MCBS Public Use Files) |
| **Contact** | MCBS@cms.hhs.gov |

---

## 2. Who Publishes It and Under What Authority

**Publisher.** The MCBS is sponsored and published by CMS's **Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics (OEDA)**. CMS does not conduct the fieldwork itself; it contracts with **NORC at the University of Chicago**, which designs instruments, conducts interviews, processes data, and produces documentation. Historically (from 1991 into the early 2010s), fieldwork was conducted by **Westat** of Rockville, MD, for what was then CMS's Office of Strategic Planning.

**Statutory authority and mandate.** The survey is explicitly **authorized by Section 1875 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. §1395ll)**, which directs HHS to conduct studies and evaluations of the Medicare program. CMS's OMB supporting statements additionally cite the survey as necessary for compliance with:

- **Section 1115A of the Social Security Act** (added by §3021 of the Affordable Care Act, 2010) — evaluation of Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) payment and care models; and
- **Section 723 of the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act (MMA) of 2003**.

The collection is cleared under the Paperwork Reduction Act as **OMB No. 0938-0568**, subject to periodic re-approval (a transparency trail preservationists can follow via reginfo.gov and omb.report).

---

## 3. History and Evolution

- **Origins (late 1980s–1991).** Medicare (created 1966, expanded to people with disabilities in 1972–73) faced mounting costs and rapid policy change by the late 1980s. Administrative claims data could not answer questions about beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs, non-covered services, supplemental insurance, health status, or satisfaction. The MCBS was implemented in **1991** to fill those gaps: to administer the Medicare program, estimate total health care expenditures for beneficiaries (including those not in administrative records), and understand beneficiary health and well-being.
- **Design change (1994).** Originally conceived as an indefinite longitudinal panel, the survey shifted in 1994 to a **rotating panel design**: four overlapping panels, each participating for up to four years (up to ~11–12 interviews over that span), with a new panel added each fall and the oldest retired.
- **Continuous operation.** Three rounds per year — winter (Jan–Apr), summer (May–Aug), fall (Sept–Dec) — using computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI), in person and by phone. Beneficiaries are interviewed whether they live in the community (~90% of interviews) or in long-term care facilities (~10%, typically via facility-staff proxies).
- **Contractor transition and the 2014 gap.** A transition from Westat to NORC beginning in 2014 disrupted the schedule: **no 2014 data year was released**, and 2015 data collection used a modified round structure (March 2015–January 2016). This gap is a permanent feature of the time series that analysts must work around (it also affects longitudinal weights).
- **2015 redesign.** The legacy annual files — **Access to Care** (1991–2013) and **Cost and Use** (1992–2013), organized in a "Record Identification Code" (RIC) structure — were replaced by:
  - the **Survey File** (survey data plus administrative/enrollment data on health status, access, satisfaction, insurance, demographics), and
  - the **Cost Supplement File** (event-level and summary expenditure and utilization data linking claims to survey-reported events, including services Medicare doesn't cover).
  Segments are now named by topic rather than RIC codes, and demographic/survey content lives exclusively in the Survey File.
- **Public Use Files (2016–present).** CMS began releasing free, de-identified microdata PUFs in 2016 (Survey File PUFs exist for 2013 and 2015 forward; Cost Supplement PUFs for 2018 forward).
- **COVID-19 (2020–2021).** Interviews shifted to telephone in March 2020, and CMS fielded three out-of-cycle **COVID-19 Rapid Response Community Supplements** (Summer 2020, Fall 2020, Winter 2021) — 15-minute phone surveys on telemedicine, deferred care, testing, vaccination, and social/emotional/financial impacts — released rapidly as standalone PUFs and later as LDS segments.
- **Recent enhancements.** A **Survey File – Early Release** product was added to improve timeliness (2025 data available now, at $300/year). In **December 2024, all MCBS microdata PUFs were migrated to data.cms.gov**, CMS's modern open-data platform.

---

## 4. Methodology and Content (for the Data Scientist)

**Sample.** A nationally representative, stratified multistage area probability sample of the **entire Medicare population** — aged 65+, and under-65 beneficiaries with qualifying disabilities — including people in nursing homes and other institutions (a population many surveys miss). Each of four active panels contains roughly 4,000 sample persons.

**Content.** The Survey File contains **6,000+ variables**: self-reported health status and conditions, functional limitations, health insurance coverage (including supplemental/Medigap and Medicaid dual eligibility), access to and satisfaction with care, usual source of care, social determinants of health, economic outcomes, housing, medication non-adherence, and program knowledge. The LDS versions are **augmented with 5 years of enrollment data and (for FFS enrollees) 5 years of limited claims**.

**The Cost Supplement's distinctive value:** it reconciles survey-reported events with Medicare claims to capture **total** health care spending and **all sources of payment** — including out-of-pocket costs, Medicaid, private insurance, and non-covered services (e.g., dental) — something neither claims nor survey data can do alone.

**Weights.** Analysts must choose carefully: "always enrolled" vs. "ever enrolled" cross-sectional weights (the latter is required for mortality and end-of-life analyses), plus longitudinal weights (limited by the 2014 gap). Facility interviews are excluded from PUFs but present in LDS files.

**Documentation ecosystem.** CMS/NORC publish an unusually rich suite: a year-agnostic **MCBS Methodology Report**, annual Data User's Guides, Variable Crosswalks (essential for bridging the pre/post-2015 structures), codebooks, a Glossary, new-user and advanced tutorials (longitudinal analysis, year-to-year comparisons, COVID supplements), an annotated Bibliography, Chartbooks, Sourcebooks, infographics, and annual Release Notes.

**Formats.** PUFs are distributed primarily as **SAS transport (.xpt) files** with sample SAS code — a note for preservationists, since proprietary-tool-dependent formats warrant format migration planning.

---

## 5. Data Products, Access Pathways, and Costs

| Product | Years available (as of latest announcements) | Access | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Survey File – Early Release (LDS)** | 2025 now; 2026 expected summer 2027 | DUA via EPPE | $300/year |
| **Survey File (LDS)** | 2015–2024 | DUA via EPPE | $300/year |
| **Cost Supplement File (LDS)** | 2015–2023 (2024 expected fall 2026) | DUA via EPPE | $300/year |
| **Survey File PUF** | 2013, 2015–2023 | Free download, data.cms.gov | Free |
| **Cost Supplement PUF** | 2018–2023 | Free download, data.cms.gov | Free |
| **COVID-19 Supplement PUFs** | Summer 2020, Fall 2020, Winter 2021 | Free download, data.cms.gov | Free |
| **Legacy Access to Care / Cost and Use** | 1991/1992–2013 | Via ResDAC request | Fee-based |

**Access mechanics.** LDS files are "limited data sets" under the HIPAA Privacy Rule — beneficiary-level but stripped of direct identifiers. Requests require a **Data Use Agreement (DUA)** submitted through CMS's **Enterprise Privacy Policy Engine (EPPE)**; DUA processing takes roughly **6–8 weeks**. PUFs require no DUA and are community-resident-only subsets with additional disclosure-risk protections. The **Research Data Assistance Center (ResDAC)**, at the University of Minnesota under CMS contract, provides technical assistance and handles legacy file requests.

---

## 6. Typical Users

- **Federal policy and budget agencies:** the **Congressional Budget Office** (MCBS was central to its cost estimate for the Part D prescription drug benefit), the **Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC)**, the **CMS Office of the Actuary**, and the **Federal Interagency Forum on Aging-Related Statistics**.
- **CMS internally:** administering and monitoring the program, estimating eligibility for proposed CMMI models, evaluating ACA-mandated demonstrations, and supporting Medicare Trustees reporting.
- **Academic and think-tank researchers:** hundreds of peer-reviewed articles in *Health Affairs*, *NEJM*, *Health Services Research*, *JAMA*-family journals, *American Journal of Managed Care*, *Annals of Emergency Medicine*, etc. Recent examples include studies of Medigap vs. Medicare Advantage trends, opioid use among elderly beneficiaries, and out-of-pocket costs of emergency care.
- **Advocates and journalists:** analyses of affordability burdens, dual eligibles, and access disparities.

---

## 7. Benefits to the Public

1. **It's the only nationally representative source that captures what claims can't:** out-of-pocket spending, non-covered services, supplemental coverage, health status, functioning, satisfaction, and social risk factors — for the entire Medicare population, including the institutionalized and the disabled under 65.
2. **Direct policy impact:** MCBS data informed the design and implementation of the **Medicare Part D drug benefit**, ACA model evaluations, and the federal COVID-19 response for older adults (rapid supplements documented telehealth adoption, deferred care, and vaccination among the most vulnerable population).
3. **Accountability infrastructure:** it underpins cost estimates and program evaluations by CBO, MedPAC, and the actuaries — the evidentiary basis for legislative decisions affecting 60+ million beneficiaries and hundreds of billions of dollars.
4. **Longitudinal and trend capability:** 30+ years of continuous collection supports year-to-year trend measurement and four-year panels tracking "spend-down" to Medicaid, health decline, and mortality — irreplaceable for studying aging and disability policy over time.
5. **Open access:** the free PUFs (no DUA required) democratize use by students, small nonprofits, journalists, and advocates who cannot navigate the DUA process.

---

## 8. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **Known discontinuities:** the **2014 data year does not exist** (contractor transition); the 2015 redesign changed file names, segment structure, variable names, and some weight conventions — the Variable Crosswalks and methodology reports are essential preservation companions.
- **Platform churn:** PUFs moved to **data.cms.gov in December 2024**; many legacy URLs under `/Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems/Research/MCBS/` and `/files/document/` still host tutorials, memos, and methodology PDFs and are vulnerable to link rot. The CMS page itself has been reorganized under `/data-research/`.
- **Independent archiving:** ICPSR at the University of Michigan maintains an **MCBS series (series 34)** of the public-use data — an important redundant, preservation-grade copy outside the publishing agency.
- **Format risk:** SAS transport files and PDF documentation dominate; consider format migration and checksum documentation for long-term stewardship.
- **Governance trail:** OMB clearance records (0938-0568) and Federal Register notices document changes in scope and burden — useful provenance metadata.
- **Mirrors:** some MCBS PUFs have been re-hosted by state open-data portals (e.g., Virginia's), reflecting third-party preservation activity.

---

## 9. Key Sources

- CMS MCBS main page: https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey
- MCBS LDS ordering page: https://www.cms.gov/data-research/files-for-order/limited-data-set-lds-files/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey-mcbs
- MCBS Methodology Report and 2015 Methodology Report (cms.gov PDFs)
- MCBS Data Documentation & Codebooks: https://www.cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey/data-documentation-codebooks
- OMB Supporting Statement (OMB No. 0938-0568), via omb.report
- NORC project pages: https://www.norc.org/research/projects/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey.html
- ResDAC: https://resdac.org (MCBS articles and legacy file requests)
- ICPSR MCBS Series: https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/web/ICPSR/series/34/studies
- CBO, "A Detailed Description of CBO's Cost Estimate for the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit" (2003)
- LoSasso & Eppig, "A Profile of the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey," *Health Care Financing Review* (PMC4193434)

If you'd like, I can go deeper on any single facet — e.g., the full variable/segment inventory of a specific data year, the pre-2015 RIC file structure, or the regulatory history of the OMB clearances.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- ICR 0938-0568 is **active**: OMB approved the 2026 full clearance revision on **1/6/2026**, with expiration **1/31/2029** — renewed well before expiration (reginfo.gov ref 202511-0938-005).
- A further revision (ref 202607-0938-013, submitted 7/27/2026) is in process, indicating active program management, not abandonment.
- Collection and release are on their intended schedule: 2024 Survey File LDS (announced 7/6/2026), 2025 Survey File Early Release LDS (announced 9/22/2026), 2026 Questionnaire Specifications released 10/30/2026, and 2025 Early Release PUFs published. The 2024 Cost Supplement and PUFs are slated for fall/winter 2026 per the published LDS update schedule.
- No statutory deadline missed; no skipped collection cycles.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- Release lags are long (Cost Supplement ~3 years) and the schedule is explicitly "subject to change," but this is typical for MCBS, not a new delay.

**Evidence for "High Risk"/"Gone":** None found.

**Selected: No Known Issue.** Active ICR through January 2029, fieldwork ongoing, releases proceeding per the published schedule.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for "High Risk" (actual reductions in granularity/frequency):**
- The 2026 OMB clearance **reduced MCBS respondent burden by 8%**, achieved partly through **removal of survey items** and **changing item administration schedules** (i.e., asking some items less often — an item-level frequency reduction) in the Community and Facility instruments (OMB supporting statement, ref 202607-0938-013).
- A pending revision would implement **additional item deletions** starting Winter 2027 (a further ~1% burden reduction, 341 hours), per terms of clearance requiring CMS to "remove questions that are no longer relevant" and content "no longer performing well."
- Users of 2026+ files will find variables present in prior cycles now deleted or asked less frequently.

**Evidence for "No Known Issue"/improvement:**
- Frequency (three rounds/year) and sample design are unchanged; timeliness arguably **improved** with the Survey File – Early Release product (data within 8 months of collection) and new topical preliminary-estimate PUFs (internet access, appeals knowledge).
- The core 6,000+ variable Survey File and claims linkage remain intact; burden reduction is partly from text simplification that is analytically neutral.

**Selected: High Risk** — with an important caveat. Approved, in-implementation item deletions and administration-schedule changes constitute literal reductions in granularity/frequency under the rubric, even though the magnitude is modest (~9% cumulative burden reduction), the core instrument survives, and timeliness has improved. This is a "watch closely" High, driven entirely by deregulatory burden-cutting rather than any signal of program termination.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- Explicit statutory authorizations named in the ICR itself: **Section 1875 of the Social Security Act** (42 U.S.C. §1395ll), **ACA §3021** (SSA §1115A — CMMI model evaluation), and **MMA §723** (2003).
- Required for implementation of a federal program: ACA §1115A obligates evaluation of Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation models, for which MCBS is a designated data source.
- **No substitute exists**: MCBS is the only nationally representative collection linking beneficiary-reported health status, insurance, out-of-pocket spending, and non-covered services to Medicare claims for the entire beneficiary population (including institutionalized and under-65 disabled). Claims data, CAHPS, and NHIS/MEPS each cover only fragments of this.
- Clear programmatic use by CBO, MedPAC, CMS actuaries, and CMMI.

**Evidence for higher risk levels:** None found.

**Selected: No Known Issue.** Explicit statutory citations, a statutory evaluation mandate, and no viable alternative collection.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "No Known Issue" (for MCBS specifically):**
- CMS lost approximately **300 employees (~4–5% of its ~6,000+ workforce)** in the April 2025 HHS reduction in force — **below the 10% threshold**. Impacted offices (minority health, Program Operations & Local Engagement, grants/contracts management, Medicare-Medicaid Coordination Office, civil rights office) do not include OEDA; CMS's IT function was explicitly spared "because of the sensitivity of many of our data sets" (CNBC, 4/4/2025; Mintz; KFF Health News).
- MCBS funding appears intact: the pending ICR reports **$22.3 million in annual federal cost**, collection continues uninterrupted, and CMS is investing in new products (Early Release files, new PUFs) — not retrenching.
- Leadership change (Dr. Mehmet Oz confirmed as CMS Administrator, April 2025) is a routine administration transition rather than a removal signaling instability.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The **contractor environment is deteriorating**: HHS's terminated-contracts list includes NORC work (an ACF contract), and peer survey research firms have been hit hard (RTI International down >35% of workforce after ~$1.1B in DOGE contract cuts). The 2014 contractor transition already demonstrated MCBS's vulnerability to contract disruption (a lost data year).
- HHS as a whole lost ~10,000 staff (~20%), and the office managing CMS grants and contracts was cut — relevant because MCBS is contract-dependent and prior reporting warns "there are no contract staff to renew some of these contracts."

**Selected: No Known Issue** (borderline Moderate). Measured against the rubric's thresholds at the agency and program level — <10% staff loss at CMS, no evidence of MCBS budget reduction, no OEDA-specific cuts, normal leadership transition — the criteria for Moderate are not met. However, the contractor-fragility signal is real and warrants monitoring; any disruption to the NORC contract would immediately escalate this category.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for "High Risk" (Presidential Action-driven ICR):**
- The OMB terms of clearance for the 2026 approval **explicitly direct CMS to reduce MCBS respondent burden "guided by the principles and priorities set forth in Executive Order 14192, 'Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation'"** — making the current and pending ICR revisions literally Presidential Action-driven. The resulting content deletions (8% + ~1% burden reductions) are "changes in accordance with Administration priorities" affecting what data is collected.
- The administration's broader posture toward federal surveys is hostile: DOGE's **"2025 Survey of Surveys"** demanded agencies justify each collection under threat of "ADVERSE ACTIONS, INCLUDING TERMINATION," and DOGE has announced terminations of surveys it deemed wasteful (NPR/WFAE, 5/23/2025).

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- No termination, negative policy note, or substantive restructuring targeting MCBS specifically has been announced; the survey's Medicare-program focus is comparatively non-ideological and it serves functions (Medicare oversight, payment model evaluation) the current administration also uses.

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":** Not sustainable — the EO 14192-driven burden reduction directly changed collection content after January 2025.

**Selected: High Risk** — per the rubric's explicit criterion ("Presidential Action-driven ICR"). Context matters, though: this is burden-trimming of a continuing, statutorily anchored survey, not a termination signal. The risk is erosion of content (realized, modest) and the possibility that the deregulatory/survey-review apparatus escalates — not imminent disappearance.

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Data Quality | **High Risk** (approved EO-driven item deletions/schedule reductions; modest in scope, timeliness improved) |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** |
| Staffing and Funding | **No Known Issue** (borderline; watch NORC/HHS contract environment) |
| Policy | **High Risk** (ICR revisions explicitly driven by EO 14192; DOGE survey-review initiative) |

**Overall assessment:** MCBS is a structurally resilient dataset — statutorily anchored, actively cleared through January 2029, releasing on schedule, with redundant archiving at ICPSR — that is nonetheless experiencing real, presidentially directed erosion at the margins (questionnaire content deletions) and operates in a degraded federal-statistical and contracting environment. The most probable adverse scenario is continued incremental content trimming and potential contractor disruption (recall the lost 2014 data year), not wholesale removal. Preservationists should prioritize archiving the **2015–2025 pre-reduction files and their codebooks/variable crosswalks now**, since those cycles contain questionnaire items that will disappear from 2026–2027 instruments onward.
